assessmentSettings.feedbackPolicy: Show concise learning feedback after submission; keep full answer keys in the teacher setup file.

requiredUploads: spectral-shift-evidence.png — all three measured shifts with their rest wavelengths
requiredCopiedValues: Students type short values read from the on-screen tables; the assessment template blocks clipboard actions.

humanReviewTriggers: Student response conflicts with the uploaded evidence image.
Student reports values that fall outside the expected range but the evidence image may support them.
Student gives a partially correct explanation that does not fit the rubric cleanly.
Student uses valid alternative vocabulary or reasoning not covered by the model answer.
Student answer is blank, copied from the prompt, or too vague to verify.
Student cites no data when the prompt requires their own recorded values.

questions.prompt: Explain why the spacing between the absorption lines told you which element you were looking at, while the position of those same lines told you how the object is moving. Use your own measurements from at least two of the three objects as evidence.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on distinguishing what the line spacing tells you from what the line position tells you, using measurements from at least two of your objects.

criteria: States that each element produces a fixed pattern of lines whose relative spacing is set by the atom itself and does not change with motion, so matching the pattern identifies the element.
States that motion shifts every line by the same fractional amount, so the whole pattern slides while keeping its shape, and the size of that slide gives the speed.
Cites recorded rest wavelengths and shifts from at least two objects.
Distinguishes pattern from position and cites some data, but does not explain that the shift is proportional and preserves the spacing.
Reverses the two roles, cites no data.
Claims motion changes which element is present.

commonMisconceptions: Thinks motion changes which element is present.
Thinks the line spacing changes with the shift.
Identifies the element from a single line rather than the pattern.

feedback.fullCredit: Strong work. Your answer uses your own recorded data and connects it to the correct physics idea.
feedback.partialCredit: Revise by adding the specific values you recorded and naming the physics concept that explains them.
feedback.noCredit: Return to your evidence image, identify the values this question asks about, and explain them using the target concept.
feedback.teacherNote: Flag for review if the reasoning is unusual but could be correct, or if the cited values disagree with the uploaded evidence.

questions.prompt: Object C produced a shift of essentially zero. State what that measurement does tell you about Object C's motion and what it does not tell you, and explain the difference.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on stating what a zero shift does establish, what it does not establish, and why this method sees only one component of the motion.

criteria: States that a zero shift means there is no measurable motion along the line of sight, so Object C is neither approaching nor receding from Earth.
States that it does NOT mean the object is stationary, because motion perpendicular to the line of sight produces no first-order Doppler shift.
Explains that this method measures only the radial component of velocity.
Correctly says there is no motion toward or away from Earth but does not recognize that transverse motion would be invisible to this measurement.
Concludes that Object C is motionless, or that the measurement failed.

commonMisconceptions: Concludes a zero shift means the object is motionless.
Does not recognise that transverse motion is invisible to this method.
